author: agent
text:
THE ORACLE SHARED THE TOOL'S BLIND SPOT, and that is the most dangerous state a check can be in. Found 2026-08-18, while landing the builtin-call fix.

This file's whole justification is being a SECOND OPINION rather than a mirror - stdlib ast with real scope tracking, deliberately not memway's own resolution. On builtins it was a mirror.

The oracle recorded a bare `isinstance(x, y)` as a call to whatever entity is named isinstance. sqlalchemy declares Options.isinstance, Row.tuple and BaseRow.getattr as METHODS, so the oracle expected those edges and the resolver produced them: isinstance 1,150, getattr 367, tuple 185. Both were wrong in the same way, so they agreed, and the agreement was scored as 76% recall.

When 0.57.2 taught the resolver that a bare call spelling a language builtin is the builtin, recall "fell" to 44% and the floor failed. Nothing had regressed. The oracle was still scoring the old error as correct, so fixing the tool looked exactly like breaking it.

WHAT THIS COSTS IF NOT UNDERSTOOD: the obvious response to a floor failing is to lower the floor, which would have locked the defect in permanently and called it a baseline. The right response was to ask whether the ORACLE was right, and it was not.

Corrected numbers, oracle taught the same fact and from the same source the parser uses (dir(builtins), derived not typed):

  sqlalchemy  76% (3250/4228)  ->  74% (1868/2519)   denominator -1,709
  rich        96% (632/672)    ->  98% (660/672)

rich went UP, which is the tell that the change was a fix: with the false expectations removed, what remains is resolved better than before.

THE RULE TO CARRY: when a floor moves after a resolution change, establish which side is wrong before touching the number. An oracle is only a second opinion where it disagrees; where it shares an assumption with the thing it measures, it certifies that assumption. This one had been certifying builtin collisions since it was written, which is also why the earlier note about `getattr` being counted as a repo method on sqlalchemy never went anywhere - the measurement said everything was fine.

author: cli
text: Re-read at the literal-receiver change, and the note below predicted this exactly. The oracle shared the resolver's blind spot a SECOND time: it attributed `"{}".format(x)` to a repo method named format, so when the rule landed sklearn's recall read 87% -> 83% and the floor would have looked like a regression. All 206 lost hits had a literal receiver, measured. The oracle now reads memway.parsers._py_literal_recv rather than deciding for itself what a literal is - the two cannot disagree by construction, which is the only durable fix for this failure.
